[MUQATIL:18:18-21/r10] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Azka food means the tastiest food; the messenger should act discreetly so no one notices or learns their whereabouts.
[MUQATIL:18:18-21/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | God awakens them to question one another; Maksalmina, the oldest, asks how long they have slept.
[MUQATIL:18:18-21/r7] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | They guess one day or part of a day because they entered the cave in the morning and awoke near the day's end.
[MUQATIL:18:18-21/r8] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Maksalmina alone tells them their Lord knows their duration better, returning the matter to God.
[MUQATIL:18:18-21/r9] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Maksalmina proposes sending one of them to town with their coins; they send Yamliha.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175#2/r1] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd b. Jubayr says the best food is the lawful food; Yaḥyā notes that some foods of their people were not lawful to them, while another view takes it to mean the tastiest food.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175#2/r2] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The messenger should act subtly and keep their presence secret; discovery could lead to stoning or forced return to disbelief, after which they would never prosper.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r3] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | They entered the cave early in the day; seeing a little sunlight remaining made them guess that they had slept a day or part of one, then they deferred the answer to God.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r4] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | One youth is sent to town with their dirhams to buy food.

[FARRA:v2p137/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · author | reports | أزكى طعاما is interpreted as meat from an animal slaughtered lawfully, since the sleepers' people were Magians.
[MAJAZ:v1p396/r6] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Baʿathnāhum means We brought them back to life, from the language of resurrection.
[MAJAZ:v1p396/r7] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Azka ṭaʿāman means more abundant food; the verse comparing seven tribes with three attests this.
[MAJAZ:v1p396/r8] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Lā yushʿiranna means let no one know about you; shaʿartu means I knew it, hence the word poet.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p400#2/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatada glosses the best food as the finest food.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p400#2/r2] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Sa'id ibn Jubayr interprets the best food as lawful food.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p400#2/r3] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · عكرمة | reports | Ikrima says it means more abundant food.
[AKHFASH:v2p429/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | فلينظر does not govern أيها directly because النظر can be followed by a question, as in انظر أزيد أكرم أم عمرو.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | God revived the sleepers from a slumber resembling death.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Wariq means silver, coined into dirhams or not; a report says ʿArfaja ibn Asʿad's silver nose became malodorous, so the Prophet ordered a gold one.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | reports | The report says the Prophet instructed ʿArfaja ibn Asʿad to replace his silver nose with gold.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | reports | Azka food can mean the greatest quantity, best quality, or lowest price; the root means growth and increase.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p265/r5] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Lā yushʿiranna means “let no one know”; the root also appears in phrases about noticing, knowing, and the perceptiveness of a poet.
[TAB-FULL:v15p161/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عمرو | reports | The youths sent one of their number to Ephesus with an old coin; the townspeople recognized its age, consulted the king and records, and rejoiced when they learned the youths' story.
[TAB-FULL:v15p196/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The youths question one another because they find their long sleep strange; some estimate a day or part of one, believing that is how long they slept.
[TAB-FULL:v15p196/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The others defer the matter to God, saying that their Lord knows best how long they remained asleep.
[TAB-FULL:v15p197/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The youths send one of their number to their former city, Ephesus, to buy food because they have awakened hungry.
[TAB-FULL:v15p197/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · وهب بن منبه | reports | Wahb says a shepherd opened the cave for sheltering sheep from rain; the youths revived the next morning and sent one with old silver to buy food, revealing their long sleep to a righteous king.
[TAB-FULL:v15p197/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · وهب بن منبه | reports | When the messenger led the king and people to the cave, terror kept them from entering; they later built a church or mosque there for prayer. | mentions 18:21
[TAB-FULL:v15p199/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عكرمة | reports | Ikrima reports that Christian youths, sons of Roman kings, withdrew from their people and slept until a Muslim community and king arose, then sought God's sign amid a dispute about bodily resurrection.
[TAB-FULL:v15p199/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عكرمة | reports | The awakened envoy's old coin exposed the era he came from, and the king presented the youths as a sign that body and soul are resurrected together.
[TAB-FULL:v15p199/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says that when people entered the cave they found bodies without souls, and the king called them a sign from God.
[TAB-FULL:v15p199/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas, passing the cave on campaign with Habib ibn Maslama, says the youths' bones had already vanished more than three hundred years later.
[TAB-FULL:v15p200/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن إسحاق | reports | Ibn Ishaq's account places the awakening under the righteous king Theodosius, whose reign lasted sixty-eight years and whose people split over belief in the Hour.
[TAB-FULL:v15p200/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن إسحاق | reports | The disputants included believers and deniers who claimed only souls, not bodies, would be raised and forgot scripture; falsehood gained ground over the believers.
[TAB-FULL:v15p200/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن إسحاق | reports | Theodosius withdraws, wears sackcloth, sits on ashes, and prays in grief for a sign to resolve the dispute.
[TAB-FULL:v15p200/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | God intends the youths' appearance to establish the Hour and bodily resurrection as truth, answer Theodosius' prayer, preserve his faith and rule, and gather dispersed believers.
[TAB-FULL:v15p200/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | God inspires Olyas to remove the stones from the cave entrance for a sheep pen; terror keeps people at a distance while the youths sit up revived, greet each other, and pray unchanged.
[TAB-FULL:v15p202/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | After prayer, the youths ask Yemliha what happened and estimate their sleep as a day or part of one; he says Deqianus seeks them and will force sacrifice or kill them.
[TAB-FULL:v15p202/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مكسلمينا | reports | Maksalimina urges them to face death without abandoning belief in God or the life after death.
[TAB-FULL:v15p202/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | They instruct Yemliha to go secretly to town, learn what is said about them, and bring more food; he takes their old coins and sees the cave entrance has been unsealed.
[TAB-FULL:v15p202/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | The youths think they have slept only their usual night and still believe Deqianus is seeking them, unaware that 309 years have passed.
[TAB-FULL:v15p203/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | Yemliha sees Christian signs displayed at the city gates and hears people openly invoking Jesus, unlike the persecution he remembers; the changed city leaves him bewildered.
[TAB-FULL:v15p203/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | He asks a local youth the city's name and learns it is Ephesus, yet fears he has lost his mind and tries to leave unseen.
[TAB-FULL:v15p203/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | When Yemliha offers an ancient coin for food, sellers pass it around and suspect he has found a buried treasure from long ago.
[TAB-FULL:v15p204/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | The townspeople accuse Yemliha of hiding a treasure, threaten to take him to the ruler, bind him, and parade him through the streets as a stranger.
[TAB-FULL:v15p204/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | They bring him to the city's two righteous governors, Arius and Astius; he believes he is being taken to Deqianus and cries to God for help.
[TAB-FULL:v15p204/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | Yemliha fears separation from his brothers and recalls their pledge never to forsake faith or one another in life or death.
[TAB-FULL:v15p206/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The city they fled was Ephesus, and the youths woke from their long sleep hungry, so they asked for food.
[TAB-FULL:v15p206/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | When Yamlīkha returned with the old coin, two city officials suspected he had found a treasure; he said it was his fathers’ currency and could not explain his situation.
[TAB-FULL:v15p206/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | No one recognized Yamlīkha or his father; some called him mad, while the officials accused him of lying and threatened torture until he confessed.
[TAB-FULL:v15p206/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | Asked about Daqyanus, the townspeople said no such man lived and that the king had died long ago; Yamlīkha realized centuries had passed.
[TAB-FULL:v15p206/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | Yamlīkha said he had seen Daqyanus enter Ephesus the previous evening,

[TAB-FULL:v15p208/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | They found Areus and the townspeople at the cave instead; Yamlīkha told the youths what happened, and they understood God had awakened them as a sign of resurrection.

[TAB-FULL:v15p211/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير | reports | The old coins dated from a king three hundred and nine years earlier; the merchant took Yamlīkha to the Muslim king, and the account matched an archived tablet.
[TAB-FULL:v15p211/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | Medinan and some Iraqi readers pronounce ورقكم with fatḥa on wāw and kasra on rāʾ; most Kufan and Basran readers make rāʾ quiescent.
[TAB-FULL:v15p211/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | Some Meccan readers kasrate rāʾ and assimilate qāf into kāf; all readings carry the same meaning and reflect known Arabic forms.
[TAB-FULL:v15p211/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | The original form is ورق with wāw fatḥa and rāʾ and qāf kasra, so al-Ṭabarī prefers that reading while accepting the others as sound forms of Arabic.
[TAB-FULL:v15p212/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مقاتل | reports | A report transmitted from Muqātil identifies the youth sent with the coins as Yamlīkh.
[TAB-FULL:v15p213/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عكرمة | reports | ʿIkrima interprets أزكى طعاما as asking which resident has the most food.
[TAB-FULL:v15p213/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd ibn Jubayr interprets أزكى طعاما as asking which food is more lawful.
[TAB-FULL:v15p213/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda gives the sense as asking which food is better.
[TAB-FULL:v15p213/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Ṭabarī prefers lawful and pure food: requiring the best makes sense whether a seller has much or little, and lawful good food outweighs abundant unlawful food.
[TAB-FULL:v15p213/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | The more-food interpretation draws on Arabic usage where zakā can mean increase; an unnamed poem uses أزكى to mean more, but al-Ṭabarī says that does not decide the verse’s sense.
[TAB-FULL:v15p213/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | أيها is grammatically attached to the city but means its inhabitants, since listeners understand that the food belongs to people.
[TAB-FULL:v15p213/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | The youths may have meant which food was lawful because they had left an idolatrous people and would not permit themselves to eat their sacrificial meat.
[TAB-FULL:v15p214/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير | reports | رزق means food or sustenance to eat.
[TAB-FULL:v15p214/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The messenger should act gently and cautiously while shopping, traveling, and entering the city, and ensure no one learns about the youths.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Wariq has four vowel patterns, with kasra on wāw the least acceptable; qāf may assimilate into kāf.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | أيها is nominative as a topic meaning which inhabitants of the city; أزكى is its predicate and طعاما a specification.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | أزكى طعاما may mean lawful food, since most townspeople were Magians who did not properly slaughter animals, or food not obtained unlawfully.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p275/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | A second interpretation is food not taken by usurpation or from an illicit source.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p276/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | In فليأتكم, the lām is read with sukūn; kasra is permitted.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p276/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | ولا يشعرن بكم means let no one know of you; if the messenger is discovered, he should not expose his companions to danger.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r1] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · ابن كثير ونافع وعاصم | reports | Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, and ʿĀṣim pronounce the thāʾ distinctly in every occurrence of كم لبثت/لبثتم; the other four readers assimilate it. | mentions 18:19
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p388/r5] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | reports | Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ kasra rāʾ in bi-wariqikum; Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, and Abū Bakr quiesce it. A report describes Abū ʿAmr's form as assimilated.
[NAHHAS:v2p451/r1] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | ‘Thus We raised them’ means We woke them, and ‘so they might ask one another’ means each would ask the others.
[NAHHAS:v2p451/r10] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The lām in li-yaʾtikum and li-yatalaṭṭaf may be read with kasra, its original vowel.
[NAHHAS:v2p451/r2] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Libtum is an allowed assimilated form because the two articulation points are close.
[NAHHAS:v2p451/r3] NAHHAS, d. 338 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Reporting from Ibn Abbas, he says one youth estimated a day and another about a day; their leader warned that disagreement brings ruin.
[NAHHAS:v2p451/r4] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أهل المدينة | reports | They assimilate the final bāʾ in ‘with your silver’; Ibn Kathir also assimilates qāf into kāf.
[NAHHAS:v2p451/r5] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أهل الكوفة وأبو عمرو | reports | They omit the kasra in ‘with your silver’ because it is heavy.
[NAHHAS:v2p451/r6] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الفراء | reports | He records a form with kasra on wāw, like kibid and fakhidh.
[NAHHAS:v2p451/r7] NAHHAS, d. 338 · نحوي غير مسمى | reports | Another grammarian says silver can be called riqqa, from warqa with its initial wāw deleted.
[NAHHAS:v2p451/r8] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | ‘Which one is purer’ means which town’s people or food; the phrase has an understood ‘people.’
[NAHHAS:v2p451/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · ابن عباس | reports | As reported by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, the youths sought the cleanest food because the townspeople slaughtered pigs.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p222/r4] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | reports | The kasra form of ورقكم preserves its original vowel; sukūn avoids the succession of repeated kasras.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p135/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم | holds | They read بورقكم with kasra on rāʾ; Abu Amr, Hamza, and Abu Bakr from Asim use a quiescent rāʾ, and a report from Ruh describes assimilation.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p135/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Both ورق and ورق are regular vowel variants; assimilating qāf into kāf is good because qāf is farther back and the following kāf nearer the mouth, favoring this direction of assimilation.

[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p24/r4] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · أبو حاتم | reports | Abū Ḥātim reports that Ibn Muḥayṣin actually read بورقكم with assimilation; Ibn Jinnī accepts that such assimilation is permissible.

[SULAMI:v1p407#2/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو عثمان المعزي | reports | Treat people of gnosis with gentleness and spiritual novices with firmness.
